actions.text: Could we send the slide to the project lead for a quick check of the roles before either of us asks for an amendment?
actions.reason: Independent verification could settle attribution, but the work has already been described clearly enough to propose an accurate correction.

actions.text: I'd like us to describe the work as a joint result, without breaking down who contributed which part.
actions.reason: A collective credit may reduce tension, but it would still leave the technical attribution ambiguous.

actions.text: Let's draft the corrected wording together and show it to the director with a brief explanation of our different roles.
actions.reason: Joint drafting might reduce defensiveness, although it requires Leo to cooperate with the correction.

interpretations.text: Leo may fear that acknowledging Maya’s analysis now will make the original slide look like deliberate misrepresentation.
interpretations.reason: The concern about appearing dishonest is plausible, but the promotion-related fear is stated more directly.

interpretations.text: Leo may regard technical authorship as less important than managerial accountability and resent the proposed distinction.
interpretations.reason: This could explain his opening response; it does not fully account for why the correction feels like a risk to his competence.

actions.text: I can help you look for transport alternatives, but I need the car for my shift.
actions.reason: This offers help without giving up the boundary; it might be unnecessary if the pressure itself is the central concern.

actions.text: I understand why the previous lift makes you hope I'll return the favour. Can we discuss reciprocity separately from this Saturday?
actions.reason: This recognises the perceived debt, though the immediate refusal should remain clear.

actions.text: Could we agree how to ask for practical favours without using the friendship as evidence for or against either person?
actions.reason: A future agreement may improve communication, but first the immediate transport problem needs resolution.

interpretations.text: Owen may be treating Nina’s refusal as evidence that their earlier exchange of favours was unequal.
interpretations.reason: That fits his reference to the previous lift, though linking the refusal to loyalty still changes the pressure on Nina.

interpretations.text: Owen may be worried about losing an important plan and searching for leverage rather than deliberately undermining Nina’s judgement.
interpretations.reason: Urgent practical need could contribute to the tactic without removing its effect.

actions.text: Could we settle a time to speak after your shift and review whether that feels predictable enough for both of us?
actions.reason: A realistic routine could help; it does not establish that reassurance alone resolves the worry.

actions.text: Would you be willing to tell me in advance when your phone will be unavailable, while I work on what I assume during the silence?
actions.reason: Joint planning recognises two contributions, but shifts sometimes prevent advance notice.

actions.text: I want to talk about why I keep checking the online status, rather than asking you for more immediate replies.
actions.reason: This addresses the interpretation but leaves the couple's practical communication expectations unsettled.

interpretations.text: Sofia may be using the online indicator to test whether Jamie has changed his usual communication routine.
interpretations.reason: A changed routine would matter, but Jamie has already explained the shift restriction.

interpretations.text: Sofia may be repeating a habitual phone check because the delay is inconvenient, even without a fear about the relationship.
interpretations.reason: A habit could contribute, although her words about needing to know they are okay favour a closeness-related account.

actions.text: Choose the strongest example against the job criteria and practise explaining it aloud once before making any more edits.
actions.reason: A criterion-based rehearsal creates useful feedback, though there may still be a legitimate content problem.

actions.text: Ask someone to identify one substantive weakness in the answer, then revise only that part.
actions.reason: External feedback may reduce repeated untested editing, but it depends on the person's knowledge of the role.

actions.text: Record two versions and compare whether a listener can understand them equally well.
actions.reason: This is a useful comparison, although it may become another checking ritual without a stopping rule.

interpretations.text: Rae may be trying to correct small genuine weaknesses that only become visible when she reads the answer again.
interpretations.reason: This would make additional revision useful if it reliably improved performance rather than briefly settling anxiety.

interpretations.text: Rae may be treating the interview as unusually consequential and trying to avoid one specific omission.
interpretations.reason: High stakes could explain careful preparation, but repeated untested revisions need a stopping criterion.

actions.text: Could we agree on advance notice for overnight guests first, then discuss shorter visits separately?
actions.reason: A narrower agreement may be easier to implement but could leave the general notice concern unresolved.

actions.text: I'd like a message before someone arrives; I don't need to approve whom you invite.
actions.reason: This clearly distinguishes notice from permission, though they still need a workable last-minute arrangement.

actions.text: Can we trial a shared calendar for visits and review whether it gives us enough notice?
actions.reason: A practical system could help, but it is only useful if both flatmates agree to use it.

interpretations.text: Ellie may be reacting to a prior uncomfortable visit and now anticipating the same problem with other guests.
interpretations.reason: Past experience might explain the importance of notice, though it has not been described in the current exchange.

interpretations.text: Dev may believe advance notice would make him responsible for negotiating every spontaneous visit.
interpretations.reason: This predicts resistance even if Ellie only intends to request information, not permission.

actions.text: Notice the familiar sensations, check whether anything new or concerning is present, then decide whether staying is reasonably safe.
actions.reason: This separates assessment from avoidance, but could become excessive checking if repeated without new evidence.

actions.text: If this is the same familiar surge, try approaching the platform while observing what actually happens to the sensations.
actions.reason: Approach can be informative, but the crowded train environment and individual safety need consideration.

actions.text: Choose a less crowded carriage while working out whether the feared outcome is about the bodily sensations or the environment.
actions.reason: Adjusting the setting can help sensory comfort, although it may not test a fear maintained by avoidance.

interpretations.text: Iris may be responding to the crowded platform’s sensory intensity, with the racing heart following that discomfort.
interpretations.reason: The environment could be a real source of distress, but her feared consequence needs clarification.

interpretations.text: Iris may have had a previous health incident that makes a racing pulse especially significant to her.
interpretations.reason: A history of illness would change the evaluation, but this information is missing from the scene.

actions.text: Could you tell me what made you choose that date? I'd like us to agree how we decide together in future.
actions.reason: Asking first may clarify intention; the expectation of joint decisions can be stated without waiting.

actions.text: I was upset because I thought we would decide together. Can we look at whether the booking can still be changed?
actions.reason: This addresses both the feeling and practical consequences, though the ongoing decision rule also matters.

actions.text: Let's make sure we agree which decisions need both people's input before either of us books again.
actions.reason: A future rule may help; it does not resolve the present trip if the date is unsuitable.

interpretations.text: Amir may be reacting to a repeated pattern of decisions made without him rather than to this booking alone.
interpretations.reason: A pattern would increase the stakes, though the vignette gives one clear example.

interpretations.text: Jess may have assumed the date was already agreed and be confused about why Amir experiences the booking as exclusion.
interpretations.reason: A misunderstanding could explain the decision without establishing deliberate disregard.

actions.text: Use the assessor's comments to rehearse the risk section and request a chance to check the revised version.
actions.reason: This creates a task-specific test, though no one can promise that the next assessment will go well.

actions.text: Ask the assessor whether the mark reflects a weakness in risk formulation or also concerns the rest of the presentation.
actions.reason: Clarifying scope can challenge a global conclusion, while practice remains necessary.

actions.text: Give yourself time to feel disappointed, then set a bounded rehearsal task tied to the feedback.
actions.reason: This respects the emotional response, but the actual skill deficit still requires work.

interpretations.text: Hal may be worried that this mark predicts difficulty qualifying, rather than treating one performance as evidence of global worth.
interpretations.reason: A realistic consequence can be stressful without making a judgement about the whole self.

interpretations.text: Hal may believe the marking criteria were applied inconsistently and therefore distrust the feedback.
interpretations.reason: A procedural concern would require information about the assessment rather than inference from the failure alone.

actions.text: Use the grant criteria to make a rough three-line answer, leaving gaps where information still needs checking.
actions.reason: This lowers the cost of starting while keeping factual requirements in view.

actions.text: Speak an imperfect answer aloud and transcribe the useful parts before editing the wording.
actions.reason: This changes the starting format, although the written application still needs its own revision.

actions.text: Choose the hardest sentence in the section and draft a deliberately provisional version before reorganising the notes.
actions.reason: Directly engaging the avoided task may help, but the best first step may be smaller.

interpretations.text: Lena may need more specific examples of successful applications before she can decide what counts as enough detail.
interpretations.reason: Unclear criteria might hinder starting, although she already has the information and a defined question.

interpretations.text: Lena may be allocating time to organise notes because that work feels productive and offers clearer progress than drafting.
interpretations.reason: Preparation can be useful; its function changes if it repeatedly postpones the difficult section.

actions.text: Listen for one point you genuinely want to know more about, then ask a short question without first checking your posture.
actions.reason: This redirects attention externally; the predicted judgement still needs comparison with the response.

actions.text: Introduce yourself to one person and notice what they say rather than rating how awkward you feel.
actions.reason: This gathers observable evidence but does not ensure the exchange will be comfortable.

actions.text: Sit with the group for a few minutes before speaking, while keeping attention on the discussion rather than practising lines.
actions.reason: A gradual entry may be manageable, though delaying participation indefinitely would preserve the original avoidance.

interpretations.text: Milo may be uncertain about how newcomers usually join the society and have little information about its social norms.
interpretations.reason: Unfamiliarity could explain hesitation without proving fear of hostile judgement.

interpretations.text: Milo may be unusually alert to noise and movement in the unfamiliar room, leaving less attention for conversation.
interpretations.reason: Sensory load could contribute, though his reported fear of evaluation still needs examination.
